title: Why is learning to read in English particularly hard?
author: Amy Coombe
summary: Amy Coombe uses her own son's first year of learning to read to ask why English is so hard to decode. She traces the problem to English's layered history, in which five languages and their spelling systems were superimposed with no reform, making it one of the most opaque writing systems in existence. She contrasts it with transparent systems such as Finnish, where children learn to read and spell in a year or less. Her core framework is that English has one sound with many spellings, one spelling with many sounds, and one word with many meanings. She uses the example of the /ee/ sound, which can be spelled ten ways, and the fact that there are 176 common spellings for 44 phonemes. The practical conclusion for reading leaders is to stop blaming the child when instruction fails, to question the earlier teaching, and to resist quick fixes in favour of expert, explicit teaching.
points: English is opaque because five spelling systems were layered on top of each other over 1,500 years with no reform, unlike transparent systems such as Finnish.
The difficulty has three parts: one sound with many spellings, one spelling with many sounds, and one word with many meanings.
With 176 common spellings for 44 phonemes, children must be taught patterns and probabilities rather than left to infer them.
When a child struggles, reading leaders should question how effective the previous instruction was instead of attributing the difficulty to the child.
More exposure to books is not a fix; something this complex needs expert, explicit teaching.
quotes: English has evolved over roughly 1500 years and, due to several invasions, consists of five different languages and their spelling systems, all of which have been superimposed upon one another: Anglo-Saxon, Danish, Norman French, Classical Latin and Greek.
It’s what’s called a ‘transparent writing system’ because letters usually represent the same sounds, and sounds are usually represented by the same letters.

A child needs to know that the letter ‘o’ does not always represent the same sound and, in this word, the letter ‘o’ represents the ‘long’ vowel sound, as in ‘post’, not the ‘short’ vowel sound as in ‘hot’.

There are 176 common ways to spell the 44 phonemes! And, in order to learn the different combinations, we need to be taught the patterns and probabilities that help us navigate this complex relationship between letters and sounds.
As we learn vocabulary, we need to learn, over time, that a single word can have several meanings, and that the meaning changes depending on the context in which it is used.

Recognising the complexity of learning to read in English helps us as reading leads to avoid the pitfall of attributing the reading difficulty to the child; it requires us to question how effective the previous instruction was and seek alternative means of teaching that child to read.
It also helps us avoid the pitfall of seeking quick fixes or believing that simply more exposure to books will be sufficient. Something so challenging requires expert, explicit teaching.
